client: Hey Luna, I've been really stressed out lately. Ever since I failed that important exam, I can't stop worrying about my academic future and whether I can keep my scholarship. It feels like everything is riding on this, and I'm not sure if I can handle the pressure.
therapist: I can hear how much this is weighing on you, and it’s completely understandable to feel stressed about your academic future and scholarship. It sounds like you’re under a lot of pressure. What are some of the thoughts that come up for you when you worry about this?

client: When I think about it, I just feel so overwhelmed. I worry that if I don’t get this scholarship, I won’t be able to afford the next semester, and that just adds to the anxiety. It’s hard to focus on my studies when I’m constantly stressed about it.
therapist: It sounds really overwhelming, and it’s natural to feel anxious when so much feels at stake. It’s understandable that these worries are making it hard to focus. Have you noticed any specific thoughts or beliefs that come up often when you’re feeling this way?

client: Yeah, I feel like I'm constantly thinking that I'm not good enough, that I'll mess things up, and that everyone will be disappointed in me. It's hard to shake those thoughts, and they just keep coming back. I've tried to push them away, but it doesn't seem to help much.
therapist: It sounds like those thoughts are really persistent and can be very tough to shake. It’s understandable to feel like you’re not good enough or that you might let others down, especially when you’re under so much pressure. Have you tried any specific strategies to manage these thoughts, or is there a particular one you’d like to explore together?

client: Yeah, I've tried a few things, but they don't seem to stick. I’ve been journaling and trying to distract myself with activities, but the thoughts just keep coming back. It’s hard because I feel like I’m just not making any progress, and it’s exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like you’ve been putting in a lot of effort to manage these thoughts, and it can be really frustrating when they keep coming back. It’s completely understandable to feel exhausted and like you’re not making progress. Have you noticed any patterns in when these thoughts are most intense, or are there specific situations that seem to trigger them more?

client: Yeah, I've noticed that the thoughts are a lot worse when I'm alone or when I have a lot of free time to think. It's like my mind just spirals into all these worst-case scenarios. I guess it makes sense, but it's hard to break that cycle, especially when I feel so alone.
therapist: It makes sense that you’d notice these thoughts becoming more intense when you have a lot of time to yourself. Being alone can sometimes make it easier for the mind to spiral into those worst-case scenarios. Have you tried any mindfulness or grounding techniques to help manage these thoughts when they start to spiral? Sometimes focusing on the present moment can help break that cycle.

client: I've tried a few mindfulness exercises before, but they don't always seem to work for me. It's hard because my mind just keeps going back to those anxious thoughts, and it feels like I can't break free from them. I guess I just get frustrated when I feel like I'm not making progress.
therapist: It’s completely understandable to feel frustrated when the mindfulness exercises don’t seem to have the effect you’re hoping for. It can be really tough to break free from those anxious thoughts, especially when they feel so persistent. Have you considered trying a different approach, like cognitive restructuring, where we can examine and challenge those anxious thoughts more directly?

client: I get what you're saying, but I feel like I've tried so many different things already, and nothing seems to stick. Cognitive restructuring sounds good in theory, but I worry it might just be another thing that doesn't work for me. It's hard because I feel like I'm stuck in this loop of anxiety, and I don't know how to break out of it.
therapist: I can understand how frustrating it must feel to try so many different things and still feel stuck in that loop of anxiety. It’s completely normal to have doubts about whether new strategies will work, especially when you’ve had a lot of experience with things not sticking. Let’s take a gentle and curious approach to cognitive restructuring. We can start by identifying one specific anxious thought and gently explore it together. What’s one thought that’s been particularly persistent for you lately?

client: I’ve been really stuck on the thought that I’m going to fail at my new job. It’s been haunting me, and I keep imagining all these scenarios where I mess up and everyone realizes I’m not cut out for it. I know it’s irrational, but it feels so real. I’m not sure if breaking it down will make a difference, though.
therapist: It sounds like that thought about failing at your new job is really weighing on you, and it’s understandable that it feels so real and persistent. Even though you recognize it might be irrational, those feelings can be very powerful. Let’s take a closer look at this thought together. Can you think of any evidence that supports the idea that you might succeed in your new job, or any times in the past where you’ve handled challenges well?

client: I know you're trying to help, but it's hard to think of those times right now. I feel like every small mistake I make at work is just confirming that I’m not cut out for this. It’s tough to see the positive when I’m so worried about messing up.
therapist: I can understand how challenging it is to see the positive when you’re feeling so worried about making mistakes. It’s natural to focus on those small errors when you’re under a lot of pressure. Let’s take a moment to acknowledge that feeling. Can you share a bit about a time, no matter how small, when you felt more confident or when something went well at work? Sometimes even the smallest successes can provide a different perspective.

client: I appreciate you trying to help me see things differently, but it's really hard to think of those moments right now. I feel like every time I think I'm doing well, something goes wrong, and it just reinforces my worries. I don't know if focusing on the small successes will really change how I feel.
therapist: I can really hear how difficult it is for you to shift your focus right now, and it’s completely understandable to feel that way when things keep going wrong. It’s natural for those setbacks to reinforce your worries. Let’s take a step back and explore this a bit differently. Sometimes, it can be helpful to look at the bigger picture and consider what you’ve learned from these challenges. What do you think you’ve gained from facing these difficulties, even if they feel tough right now?
